messages:
ana: quick follow-up from yesterday's RFC thread — I sketched a small proposal for how router + rollout-controller should handle automatic fallback without thrashing production caches or exploding costs

ben: fwiw this is motivated by the spike we saw when model-v2 started cold and many requests fell back to model-v1 simultaneously :facepalm:

maria: yes, saw that. two problems: cache warmup + surprise token costs when fallback opens up. Also noisy metrics made canary judge incorrectly.

ana: @maria (typo) — agreed. my idea: introduce a per-rollout "fallback budget" that gates how many fallback invocations are allowed per minute/hour per route. fallback consumes budget tokens. When budget depletes, router raises score penalty for fallback path instead of immediate open fallback.

ben: interesting. does budget live in rollout-controller or router?

ana: rollout-controller owns global state and policy, router enforces local token check. sync via light-weight state pub/sub (kafka/redis stream). keep router decision fast and local.

kai: tradeoffs? risk of silently blocking fallback when it is needed (bad) vs avoiding cascade (good). how do we surface blocked fallbacks?

ana: expose metrics: fallback_allowed_ratio, tokens_remaining, last_block_timestamp. Alert if fallback_rejections > X% AND error_rate or latency spikes. Also add trace log with why fallback was denied (budget/overload/throttle).

maria: how to account for streaming responses / multi-chunk sessions that might hit fallback mid-stream?

ana: we charge fallback tokens on first fallback decision for a user-request. for streaming we mark session as "fallback-bound" and don't charge again for subsequent chunks. prevents double-counting.

ben: give me config example pls

ana: sure — rough config for rollout-controller (YAML):

```yaml
rollout: model-v2-canary
fallback_policy:
  budget:
    window: 1m
    tokens: 200
    per_customer: 10
  penalty_on_deplete: 0.7 # multiply fallback score by this factor
  warmup_cache_grace: 120s
```

maria: warmup_cache_grace sounds useful — router can refuse fallback for X seconds after a successful warmup probe, to avoid oscillating. good.

kai: how do probes work? active or passive?

ana: both. rollout-controller can schedule lightweight synthetic probes (sampled QPS) and routers collect passive success rate + latency from real traffic. combine with EWMA to decide warm status.

ben: what about per-customer SLAs? enterprise customers might want guaranteed fallback (no budget).

ana: policy supports overrides: customer_exempt: [cust-id-123]. router checks allowlist first before budget logic.

maria: failure modes: 1) state replication lag -> temporary mismatch, 2) budget misconfig -> starve fallback, 3) rollout-controller crash -> fallback decisions become local-only. we should define safe defaults (graceful-deny vs allow).

kai: prefer fail-open for safety-critical customers, fail-closed for cost-sensitive default accounts. document behavior.

ben: one more: prefix cache (KV) warmup. if we limit fallback, we must also bias a small percentage of traffic to warm caches proactively. maybe 'cache-warm-samples: 0.5%'

ana: yep. add to config: cache_warm_sampling: 0.5% and prioritize those through model-v2 even if budget low.

maria: observability contract: rollout-controller emits events: FallbackBudgetUpdated, FallbackRejected, WarmupProbeResult. routers emit FallbackDecision with reason tags. correlate in console.

deploy-bot: Canary applied: service=llm-router env=prod rollout=model-v2-canary config_revision=2026-03-19T14:22Z

ben: next steps: @ana can you write this up as a short RFC with config examples + SLO/alert thresholds? @maria can you list SRE tests (chaos + replication lag) we need? kai please add per-cust exemption docs.

ana: will do. I'll drop RFC draft into eng-runtime/rfcs and ping here when ready. thanks all :seedling:
